title: Can a few queue-enforcing robots hold a queueing norm against line-cutting robots?
lede: how many enforcer robots hold a queue against line-cutting robots? About 5% of the crowd holds the norm against 30% cutters (memory 9, 10 people in view of each cut, stop chance 0.5), simulation agrees. Stylised: view size and stop chance are swept, not sourced.
summary: society-lineup found that committed line-cutting robots break a queueing norm at 12.7% of the crowd because bystander objection fades as cutting spreads. Here a share e of enforcer robots queue and object to cuts they see: each of L people in view is an enforcer with probability e, and each stops the cut with probability q, and unlike human objection this does not fade. With L = 10, q = 0.5, memory 9 and lone-cut human objection 0.9, the cutter share that breaks the norm rises from 0.127 with no enforcers to 0.201 at 3% and 0.277 at 5% enforcers. Holding the norm against 30% cutters takes 5.4% enforcers (9.7% with 5 people in view, 2.9% with 20); against 50% cutters, 7.7%. Only the product q·L matters to first order (q = 0.25 gives the same numbers as 0.5 with half the view). Simulation (200 people, 12 seeds) holds 0 of 12 crowds at 0.044 enforcers, 4 of 12 at the mean-field value 0.054 and 12 of 12 from 0.064. There is no hysteresis: a crowd that already cuts recovers at the same enforcer share. Stylised: L and q have no source and are swept; binary one-counter model.
